intro: Varese is the garden city of Lombardy, at the foot of the Alps between Lake Maggiore and Lake Como, its villas and parks full of trees planted in the nineteenth century. Readers have sent us five: a vast Lebanon cedar 34 metres tall and a ginkgo 365 centimetres round that turns gold in November, both on Italy's national register, and on a university campus a broad blue-grey cedar, a pair of cedars over picnic tables and a beech in autumn copper.
meta_description: Varese's great trees: a vast cedar of Lebanon and a gold November ginkgo on Italy's national register, and three old trees on a university campus.
question_meta: Varese's great trees: a vast cedar of Lebanon and a gold November ginkgo on Italy's national register, and three old trees on a university campus.
question_answer: The register cedar and the ginkgo stand a few dozen metres apart in a public garden off Viale Sant'Antonio; three more trees, two cedars and a beech, grow within a short walk of each other on a university campus in south-east Varese. All five are free to see.
question_context: Varese calls itself the garden city, and its villas and public parks hold some of the finest planted trees in Lombardy, many of them set out in the nineteenth century when exotic conifers and Asian trees were the fashion. A reader sent us two that stand a few dozen metres apart in a public garden off Viale Sant'Antonio, and both match entries on Italy's national register; another reader added three on a university campus: a broad blue-grey cedar, a pair of cedars over picnic tables and a beech that turns copper in late November. The first is a cedar of Lebanon, recorded at 34 metres tall, whose several trunks carry a dark, tiered crown so broad it fills the photograph. The second is a ginkgo, recorded at 365 centimetres round and 28 metres tall, which the reader photographed from below in November with every leaf turned butter yellow. Ginkgo is a living fossil, almost unchanged for some two hundred million years. We do not know when either tree was planted. The garden's boards may say, and if they do, tell us on the trees' pages.

faq.q: What are the monumental trees of Varese?
faq.a: A cedar of Lebanon 34 metres tall and a ginkgo 365 centimetres round, both listed on Italy's national register of monumental trees and standing in the same garden, and three trees a reader sent us from a university campus: two cedars and a beech.

faq.q: When is the ginkgo at its best?
faq.a: In mid-November, when its leaves turn butter yellow all at once, shortly before they fall.
Yes. Two stand in a public garden; the three campus trees are best seen in campus hours.

trees.story:
Italy keeps a national register of its monumental trees, and Varese, the garden city at the foot of the Alps between Lake Maggiore and Lake Como, has several. A reader sent us this one, and the register lists a Lebanon cedar here, 34 metres tall.

The photograph shows a tree that has outgrown its garden. Several trunks rise together from the lawn and carry a dark, tiered crown so broad that it fills the frame from side to side, the layered branches stepping out in the flat shelves that make a cedar of Lebanon recognisable from far away. At its foot a low fence keeps people off the roots, and in front of it the garden has set out benches, information boards and a white bench painted with a red heart, all facing the tree as if it were a stage.

Cedars of Lebanon came to Italy's gardens from the mountains of the eastern Mediterranean, and in the parks of Lombardy's villas some of the first plantings have grown into giants like this one. We do not know when this one was planted; the boards in front of it may say, and if they do, tell us here.

Sit on the heart bench and look up.

trees.name: The Ginkgo of Varese

official_register.name: Elenco degli alberi monumentali d'Italia (MASAF): Ginco, Varese

location.address: Public garden off Viale Sant'Antonio, Varese

trees.how_to_recognise: A tall ginkgo with a thick, dark, ridged trunk that opens into a ring of long horizontal limbs, fan-shaped leaves bright yellow in November.
verified_sources: Italy's register of monumental trees (Alberi monumentali d'Italia, MASAF), entry 'Ginco', Ginkgo biloba, girth 365 cm, height 28 m, 15 m from the reader's photograph
trees.story:
A few dozen metres from the great cedar of the same garden in Varese stands a ginkgo that Italy's national register of monumental trees also lists: 365 centimetres round and 28 metres tall. The same reader sent us both, in November, when this one was at its best.

In one sense ginkgo is the oldest tree on the planet, since the species has barely changed in some two hundred million years and was found by Europeans only in the temple gardens of China and Japan, from where it reached Europe in the eighteenth century. Planted in Italian parks, it became a favourite for exactly what the reader photographed, a few weeks each autumn when every fan-shaped leaf turns butter yellow at once.

The photograph looks straight up the trunk. It is thick, dark and ridged, and it opens into long limbs that reach out level in every direction, each one hung with gold against a hard blue sky. Soon after, a ginkgo drops nearly all its leaves within a few days, carpeting the ground.

"It was planted in 1865, in Mirabello villa's garden," the reader who sent it tells us, "near to the cedar of Lebanon." That date is theirs; the register does not give one.

Come in mid-November and stand right under it.

trees.name: The Cedar of the University Campus
trees.how_to_recognise: A lone cedar on a lawn edged by a low kerb, in front of a pale green building with white window frames: one dark, mossy trunk splitting into upswept limbs under a broad blue-grey crown.
trees.access: On a university campus; the reader walked up to it on the lawn. Visit in campus hours.
trees.story:
On a university campus in Varese, a reader stopped under this cedar on a grey November day and sent us four photographs of it.

It stands alone on a lawn beside a pale green building, and it has had room to grow the way cedars do when nothing crowds them. A single dark trunk, mossy on its north side, climbs a few metres and then breaks into long limbs that sweep upward and outward, carrying a crown so broad it fills the frame. The needles have the blue-grey cast that shows best on a wet day. The campus began, a reader tells us, as a psychiatric hospital in the early 1900s. Around the cedar it is generous with old trees: copper beeches drop a carpet of orange leaves on the grass in autumn, and a few steps away more cedars rise over a row of picnic tables.

The reader knows it as a cedar of Lebanon. The blue tint and the upswept limbs make us wonder whether it is an Atlas cedar, its close cousin from North Africa, so tell us which you think it is. We do not know when it was planted or how big it is around; if you have measured it, or the university keeps a record of its trees, tell us here and we will add it.

Walk all the way round it, and look up from under the lowest limbs.

trees.name: The Picnic-Table Cedars
trees.how_to_recognise: Two big cedars standing a few metres apart among wooden picnic tables on a campus lawn, the nearer one with a thick, deeply furrowed trunk and long sprays hanging low over the benches, a yellow building behind.
trees.access: On a university campus; the reader walked among the picnic tables under it. Visit in campus hours.
trees.story:
A reader walking the university campus in Varese sent us this pair of cedars, a short walk from the lone cedar on the lawn that they had sent us the same day.

Here the cedars grow together. Two trunks rise a few metres apart from a floor of fallen needles, and the nearer one is the giant: thick, furrowed in long plates of brown bark, with a skirt of moss at its foot. Above the picnic tables the two crowns merge into one roof of long, drooping sprays, so that on a grey November day the benches beneath sit in a green half-light. Behind them a copper beech glows orange and a yellow campus building shows through the branches.

"Among other beautiful Beech Trees, Cedars and Magnolias," the reader wrote of this corner of the campus, which began, a reader tells us, as a psychiatric hospital in the early 1900s. We do not yet know which cedar these are, how big the trunk is around, or when they were planted. If you know, or the university keeps a record of its trees, tell us here and we will add it.

Take a seat at the table under the lowest branches and look straight up.

trees.name: The Autumn Beech of the Campus
trees.how_to_recognise: A broad, low-crowned beech standing in a carpet of its own copper leaves, just behind a tall cedar whose foot is wrapped in ivy, at the corner of a pale grey building.
trees.access: On a university campus, on the lawn beside a building. Visit in campus hours.
trees.story:
In late November the beeches on the university campus in Varese turn, and a reader sent us this one at its best.

It stands on a lawn by a pale grey building, and the photograph is taken from just behind a tall cedar, so the beech is framed by the cedar's dark trunk and blue-green sprays. That makes the colour stronger. The beech's crown is broad and low, gold at the edges and copper deeper in, and beneath it the grass has vanished under a carpet of its fallen leaves, orange from one side of the frame to the other. Several stout stems rise together from its base, the way beeches grow when they have the light all to themselves.

The reader says it stands "in the University campus among other beautiful Beech Trees, Cedars and Magnolias", and the campus is generous with old trees. It began, the reader tells us, as a psychiatric hospital in the early 1900s. The lone cedar and the pair of cedars over the picnic tables, both sent to us the same day, are a short walk away. We do not yet know this beech's age or girth; if you do, tell us here.

Come in the second half of November, when the carpet is thickest.
